site.title: Health Collection
site.description: Practical guides across Health, organized for fast browsing and comparison.

pages.title: Antibiotics and viral illness
pages.summary: Antibiotics cannot cure colds, influenza or other viral infections because they are designed to disrupt bacterial structures and processes that viruses do not possess. Taking one for an uncomplicated viral illness will not kill the virus or reliably shorten the illness.

pages.title: Corrections that stick
pages.summary: A correction - a debunking, in the research vocabulary on misinformation; its pre-emptive cousin is prebunking - is most likely to stick when it gives the accurate account a clear advantage in attention, explanation and memory.

pages.title: Do corrections work
pages.summary: Corrections usually work: after people see a credible factual correction, their belief in the false claim generally falls. The original misinformation may still influence memory, interpretation or behaviour, and a correction may be weaker among people strongly committed to the claim.

pages.title: Fact checks and votes
pages.summary: Fact-checks often make political beliefs more accurate without changing how people vote. The evidence for this pattern is reasonably strong: experiments conducted during elections have repeatedly found that participants accept at least part of a correction while retaining much the same view of the candidate or policy involved.

pages.title: Health myths real decisions
pages.summary: Health myths become dangerous when they move from screens into decisions: declining vaccination, demanding antibiotics for viral illness, spending money on unsupported “brain training”, or delaying appropriate care. The evidence does not suggest that everyone who encounters misinformation acts on it.

pages.title: How to check a claim
pages.summary: Before sharing a doubtful claim, pause and run four checks: define it, trace it, test it and compare it - the fact-checking routine that professional fact-checkers call lateral reading. Write down the exact factual assertion. Trace the quotation, image, statistic or study to its earliest available source.

pages.title: Myth check
pages.summary: Myths and misconceptions are not simply foolish beliefs held by poorly informed people. They are ordinary products of human memory, reasoning and social life. A myth is usually a widely shared explanatory story or claim; a misconception is an inaccurate understanding held by an individual or group.

pages.title: Repeated messages and false consensus
pages.summary: Repeated messages can create a false impression of social consensus, especially when their common origin is hidden. The evidence for this mechanism is strong in controlled experiments and plausible in digital networks, but it does not mean that users automatically believe whatever appears popular.

pages.title: Studies versus headlines
pages.summary: To test whether a study supports a headline, compare the strength of the headline’s claim with what the researchers actually did and measured. Find the original paper, identify its design, population, comparison and main outcome, then check the size and uncertainty of the result.

pages.title: The retracted vaccine paper
pages.summary: In 1998, The Lancet published a case series describing 12 children with developmental and intestinal symptoms. Its authors proposed further investigation of a possible connection with the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, commonly called MMR.

pages.title: Verifying viral media
pages.summary: To verify a viral photograph or video, do not begin by hunting for strange fingers, shadows or pixels - begin instead with the fact-checker's core tools, reverse image search and source tracing.

pages.title: When claims outlive their sources
pages.summary: A claim can outlive the information that told us how to judge it. Memory may preserve the basic proposition—“product X causes illness”, for example—while losing the fact that it appeared in satire, came from an unreliable source or was explicitly corrected.

pages.title: Why repeated claims feel true
pages.summary: Repeated claims can begin to feel true even when repetition adds no evidence. Psychologists call this the illusory truth effect: encountering a statement before makes it easier to process, and that ease can be mistaken for accuracy. The effect is reliable but not magical.
